source.title_on_document: AI-assisted design synthesis and human creativity in engineering education

supplement.holds: Appendix A (photographic documentation of the workshop set-up, p. 4) and Appendix B (the pre- and post-surveys, p. 5). The main text cites both appendices, but neither is in this PDF. No additional statistics are said to be in the supplement; all reported test statistics are in the main text (p. 5).

paper_design_summary: Volunteers at a 90-minute engineering workshop (postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, industry mentors) self-organized into teams of two to three, and each team drew a sealed envelope that assigned it to ChatGPT-4 access (7 teams) or no LLM access (5 teams) for a 45-minute catapult design-and-build challenge. The team-level outcomes (number of designs considered, variety, uniqueness, and how well the catapult worked) come from the teams' own answers on a post-survey, and individual creative self-perceptions were measured before and after the task.

studies.label: Catapult Challenge workshop (AI-assisted vs non-AI teams)

assignment.what_was_assigned: Team condition: AI-assisted (browser access to ChatGPT-4 plus a standardized prompt sheet) versus non-AI (sketching and non-LLM web resources only). Teams self-organized before assignment; the paper calls the design quasi-experimental because team formation was not randomized.
assignment.quote: the session chair prepared 12 shuffled, opaque envelopes (seven designated as "AI group" and five designated as "non-AI group"), and immediately before the task, one representative from each self-organized team drew an envelope
assignment.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 7, Section 4 ("The condition assignment was randomized at the team level"); p. 8, Section 5

arms.name: AI-assisted teams
arms.description: Uninterrupted browser access to ChatGPT-4 (web version 2025-03-13) and a standardized prompt sheet asking for three catapult concepts with mechanical principle, ASCII sketch, and improvement tip; teams free to refine, modify, or disregard suggestions. Counts given are teams (7), not people.

arms.name: Non-AI (control) teams
arms.description: Could sketch freely and consult non-LLM web resources such as Wikipedia or YouTube; large language models prohibited. Counts given are teams (5), not people.

participants.exclusions: None reported. Counts are teams: 12 envelopes, AI = 7 teams, non-AI = 5 teams (pp. 4-5). The number of people is not stated. Teams had two to three members, so at most 36 people. Internal inconsistency: Section 2.1 says participants "self-organized into eight teams" (p. 4), while the envelopes and the results give 12 teams (7 + 5) (pp. 4-5).
participants.who: Convenience cohort of volunteers: postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors; 85% engineering background, 62% male, 30% under 34 and 70% aged 45 or older.
participants.country: not_stated (authors at Nazarbayev University, Astana; ethics statement cites the national data protection laws of the Republic of Kazakhstan, p. 8)
participants.quote: A convenience cohort of volunteers, comprising postgraduate students, early-career lecturers, and industry mentors, self-organized into eight teams of two to three members each.
participants.locator: p. 4, Section 2.1; p. 5, Section 3 ("The sample size is AI = 7 teams; non-AI = 5 teams.")

ai_tool.how_used: Teams had uninterrupted browser access to ChatGPT-4 during the 45-minute task plus a standardized prompt sheet: "Suggest three distinct catapult concepts using only craft sticks, rubber bands, and a spoon...". Teams retained full autonomy to refine, modify, or disregard suggestions (p. 4).

task.description: Catapult Challenge: design and build a functional tabletop catapult that launches a marble at least 50 cm, using an identical kit (craft sticks, rubber bands, plastic spoons, masking tape, marble, scissors, measuring tape), with a testing station available.
task.duration: 45 minutes (inside a 90-minute workshop with ~10-minute pre- and post-surveys)

outcomes.name: Quantity (fluency): number of catapult designs the team considered
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Team-level post-survey item "How many catapult designs did your team consider?" on a 5-point scale (1 design to 5+ designs). Two raters transferred categorical survey responses to a coding sheet (kappa = 0.94); they did not rate the designs.

contrasts.reported: Non-AI 60% (3 out of 5) considered three or more designs vs 0% of AI-assisted teams; U = 6, p = 0.073, effect size r = -0.52. Figure 1: AI 14.3% one design, 85.7% two designs; non-AI 40.0% two, 40.0% three, 20.0% four designs. Not significant at alpha = 0.05.

outcomes.name: Variety (flexibility): whether the team's designs used different mechanical principles
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Team-level post-survey item "Did designs employ different mechanical principles?" (0 = no variety, 1 = medium variety, 2 = distinct variety). Variety is within one team's designs.

contrasts.reported: Text: "40% vs. 29% achieving distinct principles with U = 11.5, p = 0.373, and r = -0.26". Figure 2 (left): non-AI 40.0% no variety, 20.0% medium, 40.0% distinct; AI 57.1% no variety, 42.9% medium, 0% distinct. The text's 29% for AI teams does not match Figure 2.

outcomes.name: Uniqueness (originality/novelty) of the final design
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Team-level post-survey item "How unique was your final design?" (0 = standard design, 1 = somewhat unique design, 2 = unique design). The paper also calls it "perceived design originality".

contrasts.reported: Non-AI 40% rated their final design "very unique" vs 14% (1 out of 7) of AI teams; U = 8.5, p = 0.168, r = -0.40. Figure 2 (right): non-AI 20.0% standard, 40.0% somewhat unique, 40.0% unique; AI 71.4% standard, 14.3% somewhat unique, 14.3% unique.

outcomes.name: Quality (usefulness): how well the final catapult worked
outcomes.question: with_ai
outcomes.measure_detail: Team-level post-survey item "How well did your catapult work?" (0 = failed, 1 = worked somewhat, 2 = worked well). The paper does not report an independent test-distance measurement; the outcome is the team's survey answer.

contrasts.reported: All non-AI teams (100%) "worked well" vs 29% (2 out of 7) of AI-assisted teams; U = 5.0, p = 0.051, r = -0.56. Figure 3: AI 71.4% worked somewhat, 28.6% worked well; non-AI 100.0% worked well.

outcomes.name: Individual creative self-perceptions (creative self-efficacy, divergent-thinking confidence, problem-solving efficacy, innovative-thinking ratings), pre to post
outcomes.question: none
outcomes.measure_detail: Four-item creative self-efficacy scale (three- to five-point Likert) and single-item self-ratings adapted from the 4C Creativity Assessment, measured before and after the task; within-cohort Wilcoxon signed-rank tests.

contrasts.reported: Pre- to post-task changes "were minimal in both conditions (Wilcoxon |z| < 1.2, p > 0.20 for all comparisons)".

eligibility.reason: Condition was assigned at random by envelope draw at the team level (p. 4), although the authors label the design quasi-experimental because teams self-organized. The paper gives no count of people: 12 teams of two to three members (at most 36 people; Section 2.1 also says eight teams), well under 50. All creativity outcomes are the teams' own answers on a post-survey (p. 4-5), and the authors call them self-reported measures (p. 7), so no outcome is scored on the output by raters or a computed measure.

one_line_finding: Teams with ChatGPT-4 (7 teams) reported fewer designs considered (U = 6, p = 0.073, r = -0.52), less variety (U = 11.5, p = 0.373), less unique final designs (U = 8.5, p = 0.168) and less well-working catapults (U = 5.0, p = 0.051, r = -0.56) than non-AI teams (5 teams), none significant at 0.05 (p. 5, Section 3.1; Figures 1-3, p. 6).
open_questions: Number of teams: Section 2.1 says eight teams (p. 4), but the envelope procedure and the results give 12 teams (7 AI, 5 non-AI) (pp. 4-5).
Number of people is never stated.
Variety: the text gives 29% of AI teams with distinct principles, but Figure 2 shows 0% distinct variety for AI teams (p. 5 vs p. 6).
Whether the Quality item reflects the testing-station result or only the team's own judgment; the paper presents it as a post-survey item.
The text says Uniqueness was the outcome "approaching significance" (p = 0.168), while Quality has the lowest p-value (p = 0.051).
notes: The paper calls the design "exploratory, comparative, quasi-experimental" (p. 4) because teams self-organized, but it states that condition was randomized at the team level (p. 7). I coded design_class lab_rct (supervised workshop, team-level random assignment); a reviewer may prefer quasi_people given the authors' framing. Team counts are recorded in participants with counts_are = teams; arm-level n fields are left null because they are people counts. Mann-Whitney U tests, two-tailed, alpha = 0.05, no multiple-comparison correction (p. 5, Section 2.3). Data available from the authors on request (p. 8).
